posts.title: What Happens When You Die? What the Bible Really Teaches
posts.author: Shekinah Bible Team
posts.seoTitle: What Happens When You Die? What the Bible Really Says
posts.metaDesc: What happens when you die according to the Bible? A gentle, Scripture based look at death, the resurrection, and the hope of seeing our loved ones again.
posts.excerpt: A gentle look at death, the resurrection, and the hope of seeing our loved ones again.
body: The phone call came late at night. Or maybe it was a slow goodbye in a hospital room, holding a hand that grew still. If you have lost someone you love, you know the questions that follow. Where are they now? Can they see me? Will I ever hold them again?

At the start of November, many families think about these questions even more. Toussaint and the days around it bring candles, cemetery visits, and memories of mothers, fathers, and grandparents who are gone.
The Bible does not leave us guessing. It speaks about death honestly, and it speaks about hope even more boldly. Here is what Scripture actually teaches, and why that teaching is so full of comfort.
## The short answer

The Bible teaches that when a person dies, they rest unconscious in the grave, like a deep sleep, until Jesus returns and raises them to life. The faithful do not drift as spirits or watch from somewhere unseen. Their next conscious moment will be the voice of Jesus calling them home at the resurrection (John 5:28 to 29, 1 Thessalonians 4:16).
This is the official teaching of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, and it rests on a consistent reading of Scripture from Genesis to Revelation.
## How God made us helps explain death
To understand death, start with how God created life.
> "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Genesis 2:7, KJV
Notice the formula: dust plus the breath of life equals a living soul. Adam did not receive a soul as a separate part. He became a soul. In the Bible, "soul" usually means the whole living person.

Death simply reverses that creation. "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it" (Ecclesiastes 12:7). The Hebrew word for spirit here, ruach, also means breath or wind. Job uses it the same way when he says "the spirit of God is in my nostrils" (Job 27:3). At death, the life force God gave returns to Him. The person rests.
## What the Bible says about the dead
Scripture describes the state of the dead in plain, consistent language.
- The dead know nothing. "For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing" (Ecclesiastes 9:5).
- Their thoughts stop. "His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish" (Psalm 146:4).
- They are not praising in heaven yet. "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence" (Psalm 115:17).
- They are not involved in life on earth. The dead no longer have any part in what happens "under the sun" (Ecclesiastes 9:6).
- Only God is naturally immortal. Paul says God "only hath immortality" (1 Timothy 6:16). Immortality is something He gives to the redeemed at the resurrection, not something we carry by nature.
Even King David, called a man after God's own heart (1 Samuel 13:14), is still waiting. On the day of Pentecost, Peter said plainly, "David is not ascended into the heavens" (Acts 2:34).
## Jesus called death a sleep

When His friend Lazarus died, Jesus told His disciples, "Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep" (John 11:11). The disciples misunderstood, so "Then said Jesus unto them plainly, Lazarus is dead" (John 11:14).
That was Jesus' chosen picture of death. Sleep is real, but it is not the end. You lie down expecting to wake up.

What is striking is what Lazarus did not say. He was in the tomb four days. If he had been in heaven, he would have had the greatest story ever told. Yet Scripture records no report from him, because there was nothing to report. He was asleep until Jesus called his name.

The New Testament uses this same language again and again. Stephen "fell asleep" (Acts 7:60). Paul speaks of believers "which are asleep" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Daniel describes the dead as those who "sleep in the dust of the earth" and "shall awake" (Daniel 12:2).
## The great hope: resurrection morning

If death were the whole story, this would be a sad article. It is not. The Bible's answer to death is not a ghostly afterlife. It is a resurrection, a real body, a real reunion, and a real face to face with Jesus.

> "For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air." 1 Thessalonians 4:16 to 17, KJV

Read those words slowly. Together with them. Paul wrote this to grieving believers so that they would "sorrow not, even as others which have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Christians still grieve, but we grieve with an expected reunion in view.

Paul describes the moment in 1 Corinthians 15. "In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump... the dead shall be raised incorruptible" (verse 52). Our mortal bodies will "put on immortality" (verse 53), and the whole church will sing, "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" (verse 55).

Jesus said, "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live" (John 11:25). That promise is why Job, centuries earlier, could say, "I know that my redeemer liveth" and look forward to seeing God "in my flesh" (Job 19:25 to 26).
## Why this teaching brings comfort
Some people worry that the idea of "sleep" feels cold. In practice, many grieving families find it deeply freeing.

Your loved one is not suffering or waiting anxiously. For the person who dies in Jesus, no time passes. They close their eyes, and their very next awareness is resurrection morning. Paul wanted to "depart, and to be with Christ" (Philippians 1:23) because, from the believer's point of view, death is followed immediately by Christ's appearing.

Your loved one is not watching your pain. Many people imagine a mother in heaven seeing her children struggle or a grandparent watching the family fall apart. The Bible spares them that grief. They rest in peace until God wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:4).
You do not need to fear the dead. They cannot harm you, haunt you, or demand anything from you. They are safe in God's memory.
## A word to Haitian families

Many of us grew up in homes where the dead were never far away. We heard that spirits visit in dreams, need to be fed or honored, or can bring blessing or trouble to the living. Around Fèt Gede in early November, these beliefs become especially visible across Haiti and in the diaspora.
These traditions often come from real love for those who have died and a deep longing to stay connected. That longing is good. God placed it in our hearts.

But Scripture gives a clear and loving warning. God told Israel not to consult mediums or anyone who seeks to speak with the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10 to 12). Isaiah asks, "should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?" (Isaiah 8:19). Since the dead know nothing, any voice, dream, or presence claiming to be a departed loved one is not truly them. The Bible warns that spiritual deception is real (2 Corinthians 11:14).

The good news is freedom. You do not owe the dead anything. You do not have to keep them happy or protect yourself from them. Jesus holds the keys of death and the grave (Revelation 1:18). Your loved ones who trusted Him are in His hands, and so are you.
## Questions people ask
### What about the thief on the cross?

In Luke 23:43, Jesus says, "Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." The original Greek manuscripts had no punctuation, so translators decide where the comma goes. It can be read as, "I say unto thee today, you will be with me in paradise," an emphatic promise given on the darkest day. This reading fits the rest of Scripture: on Sunday morning, Jesus Himself said, "I am not yet ascended to my Father" (John 20:17). Jesus did not go to paradise that Friday, so the thief could not have joined Him there that day. The promise was sure, and its fulfillment comes at the resurrection.
### Doesn't Paul say to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord?

In 2 Corinthians 5:8, Paul expresses his longing to be with Christ. The verses just before (2 Corinthians 5:1 to 4) explain that he is longing for his new, heavenly body, not a bodiless existence. Elsewhere Paul says his reward will come "at that day" when Jesus appears (2 Timothy 4:8). For the believer who dies, the next moment of awareness is being with the Lord.
### What about the rich man and Lazarus?

Luke 16:19 to 31 is a parable, one of a series of stories Jesus told in Luke 15 and 16 to teach a lesson. Taken literally, it would mean heaven and hell are close enough to talk across, and that a drop of water could cool a soul. Jesus used a popular story of His day to make one point: our choices in this life matter, and Scripture is enough to lead us to repentance (Luke 16:31).
### Can our loved ones see us from heaven?

According to Ecclesiastes 9:5 to 6, the dead know nothing and have no part in what happens on earth. That may feel hard at first, but it means they are spared the sorrow of watching us suffer. The joy of reunion is waiting for resurrection day.
## Reflection questions
- Which Bible promise about the resurrection speaks most to your heart right now?
- How does knowing your loved one is resting, not watching, change the way you grieve?
- Is there a fear about death or the dead that Jesus wants to lift from you today?
## A word of encouragement

If you are grieving, your tears are not a lack of faith. Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus even though He knew He would raise him minutes later (John 11:35). He weeps with you too. And He has already walked out of His own tomb. Because He lives, death is not the last word for anyone who trusts Him. One day the graves will open, families will be reunited, and death itself will be gone forever.
## A prayer

Jesus, You know what it feels like to lose someone You love. Thank You for being the resurrection and the life. Hold every heart that is grieving today. Free us from fear, and fill us with the hope of the morning when You will call our loved ones by name. Until then, keep us close to You. Amen.
## Your next step

If you are carrying grief right now, you do not have to carry it alone. Our church family would be honored to pray with you through our prayer request page. Want to explore what the Bible says about death, the resurrection, and the second coming of Jesus at your own pace? Request a free Bible study below with someone from Shekinah.

posts.title: Why Do Seventh-day Adventists Worship on Saturday?
posts.author: Shekinah Bible Team
posts.seoTitle: Why Do Adventists Worship on Saturday? A Bible Answer
posts.metaDesc: Why do Seventh-day Adventists worship on Saturday? Explore the Bible, history, and heart behind the Sabbath, plus the honest questions people ask most.
posts.excerpt: The Bible story, the history, and the heart behind Sabbath worship, plus honest answers to the questions people ask most.
body: Maybe a coworker turned down your Saturday barbecue because she had church. Maybe you drove past a full parking lot on a Saturday morning and wondered what was going on. Or maybe you grew up keeping Sunday and someone handed you a Bible verse that left you curious.

Whatever brought you here, it is a fair question, and it deserves more than a one line answer. Seventh-day Adventists worship on Saturday because the Bible names the seventh day as the Sabbath God blessed at Creation, wrote into the Ten Commandments, and Jesus Himself kept. For Adventists, it is not a rule to earn salvation. It is a weekly appointment with the God who already saved them.
Let us walk through what Scripture says, how Sunday worship became common, and what Sabbath looks like in real life.
## The short answer

Adventists keep Saturday as the Sabbath because the Bible consistently calls the seventh day holy, and nowhere in Scripture does God move that blessing to another day. The Sabbath runs from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset, following the biblical way of counting days from evening to evening (Genesis 1:5, Leviticus 23:32, Mark 1:32).
That conviction rests on five threads that run through the whole Bible.
## 1. The Sabbath began at Creation, before there were any Jews
The Sabbath is older than Israel, older than Moses, and older than sin. It started in the Garden of Eden.

> "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it." Genesis 2:2 to 3, KJV
God did three things to that day. He rested on it, He blessed it, and He set it apart as holy. He did not do this to any other day of the week.

This matters because many people assume the Sabbath was only for the Jewish nation. Yet Jesus said, "The sabbath was made for man" (Mark 2:27). The word for man there points to humanity as a whole. Adam and Eve were not Jewish. The Sabbath was a gift to the whole human family, given before any nation existed.

The official Adventist statement of belief describes the Sabbath as a memorial of Creation. Every Saturday becomes a weekly reminder that we did not make ourselves. Someone made us, loves us, and invites us to rest.
## 2. God placed the Sabbath in the heart of the Ten Commandments
When God spoke the Ten Commandments from Mount Sinai and wrote them with His own finger, the fourth commandment named a specific day.
> "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God." Exodus 20:8 to 10, KJV
Notice the first word: remember. God was not introducing something new. He was calling His people back to something He had established at Creation, and the commandment says so directly in verse 11.

Most Christians agree the other nine commandments still guide us today. We still believe lying, stealing, and idolatry are wrong. Adventists simply ask why the one commandment that begins with "remember" would be the one we forget. Jesus put it gently: "If ye love me, keep my commandments" (John 14:15).
## 3. Jesus kept the Sabbath and called Himself its Lord
Jesus never treated the Sabbath as something to throw away. He treated it as something to rescue.
Luke tells us that Jesus went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day "as his custom was" (Luke 4:16). Sabbath worship was His regular habit, not an occasional visit.

Jesus did push back against the heavy human rules religious leaders had piled on the day. He healed on the Sabbath, fed His hungry disciples, and taught that "it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days" (Matthew 12:12). He was not abolishing the Sabbath. He was restoring it to what God intended: a day of healing, mercy, and freedom.
He also called Himself "Lord also of the sabbath" (Mark 2:28). If Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath, then the Sabbath is, in a real sense, the Lord's Day.

Even at His death, His followers honored the day. After the crucifixion, the women who loved Him "rested the sabbath day according to the commandment" (Luke 23:56), then came to the tomb on the first day of the week (Luke 24:1). Scripture marks three days in a row here: the preparation day when Jesus died, the Sabbath when He rested in the tomb, and the first day when He rose.
## 4. The apostles kept worshiping on the Sabbath after the resurrection
If the resurrection had moved worship to Sunday, we would expect the book of Acts to show it. Instead, Acts records the apostles meeting on the Sabbath year after year.
- Paul and Barnabas preached in the synagogue on the Sabbath, and the next Sabbath nearly the whole city came out to hear them, including many Gentiles (Acts 13:14, 42, 44).
- In Philippi, where there was no synagogue, Paul went to a riverside place of prayer on the Sabbath (Acts 16:13).
- In Thessalonica, Paul reasoned from the Scriptures on three Sabbaths, "as his manner was" (Acts 17:2).
- In Corinth, he taught every Sabbath for a year and a half, to both Jews and Greeks (Acts 18:4, 11).

The New Testament also looks ahead. Hebrews 4:9 says, "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God." The Greek word used there is sabbatismos, a Sabbath keeping. And the prophet Isaiah pictures the redeemed worshiping God "from one sabbath to another" in the new earth (Isaiah 66:22 to 23).
## 5. The Sabbath is a sign of freedom and belonging

When Moses repeated the Ten Commandments in Deuteronomy, he gave another reason to keep the Sabbath: "remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 5:15). The Sabbath celebrates deliverance.

For Christians, that points to Jesus, who frees us from the slavery of sin. God calls the Sabbath a sign "that ye may know that I am the LORD your God" (Ezekiel 20:20). It is like a wedding ring. Wearing it does not make you married, but it shows whose you are.

This is why Adventists insist Sabbath keeping is never about earning salvation. We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus alone (Ephesians 2:8 to 9). Resting on the Sabbath is one of the clearest pictures of grace there is. Once a week we stop working and trust God to hold our lives together.
## So how did most Christians end up worshiping on Sunday?

The shift to Sunday came gradually, through church tradition and civil law, not through a command in Scripture. Most historians, including many Catholic and Protestant scholars, describe it as a development of the centuries after the apostles.
A few key moments stand out:

- Early second century onward. Some Christians began gathering on Sunday to honor the resurrection. Many historians link the growing preference for Sunday to a desire to distance the church from Judaism during a time of tension with the Roman empire.
- March 7, 321. Emperor Constantine issued the first civil law calling for rest on "the venerable day of the sun," with exceptions for farmers.
- Fourth century. The regional Council of Laodicea instructed Christians to work on Saturday and to honor Sunday instead.

Throughout those centuries, many believers kept the seventh day anyway, and Sabbath keeping never fully disappeared. In the 1840s, the founders of the Adventist movement learned the seventh day Sabbath from Seventh Day Baptists and became convinced it was a truth worth restoring.

Adventists do not believe Sunday keeping Christians are insincere or less loved by God. Millions of faithful believers worship on Sunday with all their hearts. The question Adventists raise is simply this: what does Scripture itself say?
## Is Saturday really the seventh day?

Yes. The weekly cycle has never been broken. When the Gregorian calendar replaced the Julian calendar in 1582, ten dates were dropped, but the days of the week stayed in order. Thursday, October 4 was followed by Friday, October 15.

Language tells the story too. In many languages around the world, the name for Saturday comes from the word Sabbath. Spanish says sábado. French says samedi. And in Haitian Creole, Saturday is samdi, a word that traces back through French and Latin to the Sabbath. Many Haitian families have been naming the Sabbath every week without realizing it.
## Honest questions people ask
### Does Acts 20:7 show the early church met on Sunday?

Acts 20:7 describes one farewell meeting in Troas on the first day of the week, when Paul preached until midnight because he was leaving the next morning. In biblical reckoning, the first day began at Saturday sunset, so this was likely a Saturday night gathering. Breaking bread was also something believers did daily (Acts 2:46). The passage records an event, but it does not command a new day of worship.
### What about 1 Corinthians 16:2?

Paul asked believers to set money aside "by him in store" on the first day of the week for famine relief in Jerusalem. The wording points to putting funds aside at home before the week's spending began, so the gift would be ready when Paul arrived. It is a plan for collecting relief offerings, not a description of a worship service.
### Doesn't Colossians 2:16 say the Sabbath no longer matters?

Colossians 2:16 to 17 mentions "holy days," "new moon," and "sabbath days" as a shadow of things to come. Adventists understand this list as the yearly ceremonial feasts and their special sabbaths, which pointed forward to Christ's sacrifice. The same grouping of feasts, new moons, and sabbaths appears in passages about temple offerings (Ezekiel 45:17). The weekly Sabbath points back to Creation, so it is not a shadow of something to come.
### Doesn't Romans 14:5 say every day is alike?

Romans 14 deals with disputes over food and fasting days among believers. The word Sabbath does not appear in the chapter. Paul's point is that Christians should not judge one another over personal customs. He is not setting aside one of the Ten Commandments.
### Isn't Sunday the Lord's Day because of the resurrection?

The resurrection is the heart of the gospel, and Adventists celebrate it joyfully. Yet the Bible gives baptism as the sign of the resurrection (Romans 6:4), not a change of the weekly day. When John speaks of "the Lord's day" (Revelation 1:10), the rest of Scripture identifies the Sabbath as the day the Lord calls His own (Isaiah 58:13, Mark 2:28).
## What Sabbath actually looks like
Many people imagine a long list of things you cannot do. In practice, Sabbath feels more like a weekly holiday with God.

Isaiah invites us to "call the sabbath a delight" (Isaiah 58:13). For many Adventist families, Friday evening begins with a simple worship at sunset, a warm meal, and phones set aside. Saturday morning brings Sabbath School, where people study the Bible together in small classes, followed by the worship service. The afternoon might include a walk in nature, visiting someone who is sick or lonely, or long conversations around the table. Work, shopping, and the usual chase of the week pause until sunset.

At Shekinah in Alvarado, Sabbath School begins at 10:00 AM and the Divine Service at 11:00 AM, with worship in Kreyòl and English. After service, the church family shares a meal together. For many Haitian families, the Sabbath table is where faith, culture, and community meet.
## Reflection questions
- What would change in your week if you set aside 24 hours to rest in God without guilt?
- Is your view of the Sabbath based on what Scripture says, or on what you have always heard?
- How might the Sabbath remind you that your worth does not come from your work?
## A word of encouragement

If this is new to you, you do not have to settle every question today. God is patient with honest seekers. The Sabbath is not a burden He places on tired shoulders. It is an invitation from a Savior who said, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). Open your Bible, read these passages for yourself, and ask Him to guide you.
## A prayer

Lord, thank You for making us and for loving us before we did anything to deserve it. Thank You for giving us a day to stop, breathe, and remember that we belong to You. Help me read Your Word with an open heart, and lead me into the rest that only Jesus can give. Amen.
## Your next step

We would love to welcome you for your first Sabbath. Come as you are on Saturday morning to 205 E Carver St in Alvarado, Texas. A greeter will help you find a seat, and you are invited to stay for lunch afterward. Prefer to study first? Request a free Bible study below and explore these passages one on one.

posts.title: Resting in His Presence: What the Sabbath Teaches Us About Trust
posts.author: Pastor Marc Vilmeus
posts.excerpt: In a world that never stops, God invites us into a weekly rhythm of rest that reminds us who really holds our lives.
body: Every week, as the sun sets on Friday, something holy begins. The Sabbath is not a pause from life. it is a reminder of who gives life in the first place.
When we stop working, we confess that our worth does not come from what we produce. We are loved because we are His.
This week, try setting aside one hour before sunset to prepare your home and your heart. Light a candle, read a psalm, and let the noise fade.
posts.verse: "Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.". Matthew 11:28

posts.title: Five Ways to Build Faith at the Dinner Table
posts.author: Family Ministries
posts.excerpt: Simple habits that help children see God in everyday moments. no special training required.
body: Faith is often passed down not in big moments, but in small, repeated ones. The dinner table is one of the best places to start.
Share one blessing from the day. Pray for one neighbor by name. Read one verse aloud and ask the youngest what it means.
These moments may feel small, but over years they become the foundation of a lasting faith.
posts.verse: "Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it.". Proverbs 22:6

posts.title: Eating for Life: Simple Plant Based Meals from Our Kitchen
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Haitian flavors, healthy choices. Recipes and tips from our members for nourishing the whole family.
body: Caring for our bodies is part of honoring God. And healthy food can still taste like home.
Try diri ak pwa with brown rice, legim loaded with vegetables, or a fresh mango and avocado salad.
Join us after service on the first Sabbath of each month for our fellowship lunch and recipe exchange.
posts.verse: "Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit?". 1 Corinthians 6:19

posts.title: The Gift of Rest: Why Sleep Is Part of Our Worship
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Rest, water, sunlight, and trust in God. simple habits from the Adventist health message that renew body and mind.
body: God designed our bodies with rhythms. When we honor them, we have more strength to love and serve.
Aim for seven to eight hours of sleep, drink water through the day, and step outside for morning sunlight.
Small changes, practiced faithfully, can bring lasting renewal.
posts.verse: "In peace I will lie down and sleep, for you alone, Lord, make me dwell in safety.". Psalm 4:8

posts.title: Soup Joumou, Plant Based: A Freedom Tradition for the Whole Table
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Our take on the beloved Haitian pumpkin soup. rich, hearty, and made without meat.
body: Soup joumou is more than a meal. For Haitians it is a taste of freedom and family.
Roast the squash, then simmer it with carrots, cabbage, potatoes, pasta, and epis. Add chickpeas for protein.
Share a bowl with a neighbor. Bon apeti!
posts.verse: "Taste and see that the Lord is good.". Psalm 34:8

posts.title: When Prayer Feels Quiet
posts.author: Elder Guy Jean-Louis
posts.excerpt: What to do when heaven seems silent. and why God's silence is never His absence.
body: Every believer knows the feeling: you pray, and nothing seems to change.
Scripture is full of people who waited. Hannah, David, Elijah. Their waiting was not wasted.
Keep praying. Keep showing up. God is closer than the silence suggests.
posts.verse: "Be still, and know that I am God.". Psalm 46:10

posts.title: Walk With Me: Starting a Sabbath Afternoon Walking Group
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Fresh air, good conversation, and gentle exercise. a simple way to care for body and soul together.
body: Movement is one of the simplest gifts we can give our bodies.
After fellowship lunch, join us for a 30-minute walk around the neighborhood. All ages and paces are welcome.
Bring water, comfortable shoes, and a friend.
posts.verse: "Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength." Isaiah 40:31

posts.title: Diri ak Pwa the Healthy Way
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Brown rice, red beans, and plenty of epis. the classic Haitian side dish, made lighter.
body: Few dishes say home like diri ak pwa.
Swap white rice for brown, cook the beans from dry, and season generously with epis, thyme, and clove.
Serve with a fresh avocado salad for a complete Sabbath lunch.
posts.verse: "So whether you eat or drink… do it all for the glory of God." 1 Corinthians 10:31

posts.title: Faith for the Journey: Lessons from Abraham
posts.author: Pastor Marc Vilmeus
posts.excerpt: Abraham left everything he knew with only a promise. What can his story teach us about trusting God today?
body: Abraham did not know where he was going. only who was leading him.
Many in our church family know what it means to leave home and start again.
God who called Abraham is still faithful to those who follow Him.
posts.verse: "By faith Abraham… went, even though he did not know where he was going." Hebrews 11:8

posts.title: Water First: Small Habits for Big Energy
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Before coffee, before breakfast. why a glass of water may be the best way to start your day.
body: Most of us are mildly dehydrated without knowing it.
Start each morning with a full glass of water, and keep a bottle with you through the day.
Your energy, focus, and mood will thank you.
posts.verse: "Whoever drinks the water I give them will never thirst." John 4:14

posts.title: Legim Without Meat: A Family Favorite
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Eggplant, cabbage, carrots, and chayote stewed low and slow. rich flavor, no meat required.
body: Legim is a Haitian stew that is all about the vegetables.
Sauté onions and epis, add eggplant, cabbage, carrots, chayote, and spinach, then simmer until tender.
Serve over rice or with fried plantains.
posts.verse: "Better a small serving of vegetables with love than a fattened calf with hatred." Proverbs 15:17

posts.title: Stress Less: Trusting God With Your Worries
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.excerpt: Practical steps for managing stress. rooted in prayer, rest, and community.
body: Stress affects our sleep, our hearts, and our relationships.
Take five minutes each morning to pray and breathe slowly. Share your burdens with a trusted friend.
God invites us to cast every care on Him.
posts.verse: "Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you." 1 Peter 5:7
